about.heading: About me
about.p1: I am in my second year of the BI Analyst programme at Nackademin. On the programme I have learned, among other things, to model and build data warehouses, to build reports in Power BI and to handle real-time flows in Databricks. The projects below show how.
about.p2: Before the programme I worked in healthcare, including as a nurse. That gave me a feel for how an organisation runs day to day, and which decisions the numbers are actually meant to support.
about.p3: Now I am looking for an internship (LIA) where I can test my new knowledge, between 7 December and 28 April.

project.powerbi.title: Reports in Power BI
project.powerbi.question: How is a retail company selling, which products carry the margin and which underperform?
project.powerbi.did: Several reports built on practice databases. For the invented company Himalaya Kött & Video: views for sales, HR and finance. For Freddys Bikes: reports for sales, HR and inventory. Loaded and cleaned the data, built measures in DAX, and set up tables, KPI tiles, filters and drilldowns. The layout of the sales report was designed separately in Canva.
project.powerbi.tricky: The drilldowns, and getting every table and card to interact correctly with each other when a filter is applied.
project.powerbi.outcome: A report where you filter by product or period and immediately see what sells and what underperforms. If I built it today I would start with a data warehouse and do the modelling and cleaning there rather than in Power BI.
project.warehouse.title: Data modelling and a data warehouse
project.warehouse.question: How should a data warehouse be modelled when the source data is spread across more tables than the reports need?
project.warehouse.did: Two exercises in the same course. First a bank database: modelled an ERD in draw.io and created the database with T-SQL in SQL Server. Then a data warehouse for NetOnNet: modelled a star schema in draw.io and implemented it in SQL Server Management Studio, with stored procedures and scheduled jobs against a separate source database. Reshaped the data in SQL, dates into weekdays and quarters for instance, so it could be filtered on.
project.warehouse.tricky: Holding the modelling, the keys and the naming together all the way through to the final load into the fact table, and then extending it to a snowflake schema.
project.warehouse.outcome: A working data warehouse with the schema definition in draw.io as documentation. Next time I will spend more time on the modelling before implementation starts.
project.databricks.title: Real-time train punctuality flow in Databricks
project.databricks.question: How punctual are train departures, per station and per hour? An exercise, framed as input for a train operating company.
project.databricks.did: Built a three-layer flow in Databricks. A producer in Python sends train announcements from Trafikverket’s open API to an Event Hub. A streaming job reads the hub as a Kafka source and writes the raw data unchanged into a bronze layer in Delta, with a checkpoint on the latest offset. The silver layer picks out the most recent version of each announcement. A gold job in PySpark filters to departures that actually ran, groups by hour and station, and works out the number of departures, the share punctual within five minutes, and the average and maximum delay.
project.databricks.tricky: Keeping checkpoints and offsets straight so that a restart neither loses events nor re-reads them, and making sure the same announcement does not get counted twice.
project.databricks.outcome: A gold table of punctuality per hour and station that updates as new events arrive. The raw data stays unchanged in bronze, so the whole flow can be re-run with different logic without fetching the data again.
